title: Widukind of Corvey: the battle on the Lech, 955
fact_summary: Widukind of Corvey, in his Deeds of the Saxons, describes King Otto's army meeting the Hungarians near Augsburg in 955: the Hungarians cross the river Lech and take the baggage, Duke Conrad turns the fight, the king leads the charge, and the Hungarian army is destroyed over three days.

place.label: Near Augsburg, on the river Lech
place.note: Pinned by Claude at the city of Augsburg, which Widukind names as the place near which the camp was set up. The battlefield itself is not located by the passage read.

claims.text: Widukind writes that the camp was set up “in the vicinity of Augsburg” and that the Hungarians “did not delay but crossed the Lech River”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says, read in Raymund F. Wood's English translation in the open copy linked under Sources. The Latin has not been compared yet.

claims.text: He says the king's army marched out “in number about eight legions”, with the king himself in the fifth, the “Royal Legion”, a Frankish fourth legion, and Swabian sixth and seventh legions.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says, read in Raymund F. Wood's English translation in the open copy linked under Sources. The Latin has not been compared yet.

claims.text: He says the king sent Duke Conrad with the fourth legion, who recovered the prisoners, and that Conrad “returned to the king bearing the standards of victory”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says, read in Raymund F. Wood's English translation in the open copy linked under Sources. The Latin has not been compared yet.

claims.text: A Metz annal for the same year says the Hungarians, who had entered Lothar's kingdom for the fourth time, were defeated by Otto.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: In the Latin, Widukind goes on: after a speech the king took his shield and the holy lance and “was the first to turn his horse on the enemy”. The bolder Hungarians resisted and were killed; of the rest, some were burned in the villages they fled to and others drowned swimming the river.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: He says the camp was taken that day and all the captives freed, and on the second and third day the remaining multitude was so destroyed from the neighbouring towns “that none or few escaped”. “But the victory over so fierce a people was not so bloodless.”
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: Duke Conrad, he says, fighting bravely and overheated by the fierce sun of that day, loosened his armour to catch the air and fell to an arrow in the throat. His body was carried to Worms and buried there.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: Three leaders of the Hungarian people were captured and brought before Duke Henry, and were hanged.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: Made glorious by the triumph, the king “was hailed by the army as father of the fatherland and emperor” (pater patriae imperatorque appellatus est). Widukind adds that no king had rejoiced in such a victory for two hundred years.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: The continuation of Regino's chronicle says under 955 that the Hungarians were laid low by the king's army “apud Lichum fluvium”, at the river Lech, with such slaughter that no such victory had been heard of before. A sentence printed in brackets adds: “Conrad, formerly duke, was killed there.”
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: The battle is “commonly, but less rightly, as it seems” placed on the Lechfeld.
claims.certainty_reason: An editor's note of 1882, worded as “it seems”. The study by Wyneken that it cites, and later work on the battlefield, have not been opened.

dating_methods.text: Widukind places Otto's return to Saxony, when Hungarian envoys arrived, at “about the Kalends of July”. The translator adds the year 955 in brackets, and the Metz annal puts Otto's defeat of the Hungarians under 955.
dating_methods.certainty_reason: The year rests on the translator's note and on a separate annal; the Latin text has not been checked for a year.

dating_methods.text: Widukind names no day. His editor notes that the battle he describes was fought on 10 August, and the editor of Regino's continuation prints the same day in the margin of the 955 entry.
dating_methods.certainty_reason: Two editors' dates in scholarly editions. The source that gives the day has not been opened.

open_questions.text: Widukind wrote for the victor's daughter. How much of the speech and the charge with the holy lance is report, and how much is praise?
Where exactly was the battlefield? Widukind and Regino's continuator name only Augsburg and the river Lech, and an 1882 editor already doubted the usual name “Lechfeld”.

review.note: Checked by Claude against open copies of every source. Marc spot-checks a sample.

change_notes.note: An earlier open question asked how the battle ended, because the English excerpt stopped early. The Latin edition has now been read to the end of the account and the outcome added (claims c5 to c10).
